story: On the morning of June 30, 1908, a blinding flash lit the skies over Siberia, followed by a shock wave that knocked people off their feet hundreds of miles away and flattened eighty million trees across an area of two thousand one hundred square kilometers. Yet, remarkably, it left behind no impact crater. For decades, scientists puzzled over the cataclysm, which released energy equivalent to thousands of atomic bombs. Because no large space rock fragments were initially found, wild theories emerged, ranging from comets to antimatter. Decades later, researchers discovered microscopic extraterrestrial spheres trapped in the tree resin and peat layers. The consensus today is that a stony asteroid exploded high in the atmosphere, creating a devastating air burst. It stands as the largest impact event in recorded human history, reminding us just how violently protective our atmosphere truly is.
angle: An explosion powerful enough to flatten 80 million trees across 2,150 square kilometers left absolutely no impact crater behind.

claims.claim: The Tunguska event occurred on June 30, 1908.
The explosion flattened forest across approximately 2,150 square kilometers (830 square miles).
The blast left no impact crater at the surface.
The event was caused by an atmospheric air burst rather than a ground collision.
The explosion felled an estimated 80 million trees.
Seismic stations across Eurasia and air waves were detected far away, including in Europe and the United States.
The first scientific expedition to reach the site was led by Leonid Kulik in 1927.
Later expeditions found microscopic extraterrestrial particles, silicate, and magnetite spheres with high nickel content in the soil and tree resin.
The explosive energy is estimated to be equivalent to between 10 and 30 megatons of TNT, or roughly 1,000 times the Hiroshima bomb.
Eyewitnesses reported seeing a bluish or sun-bright light moving across the sky followed by thunderous sounds and intense heat.
Night skies across Europe and Asia glowed for days after the impact due to high-altitude dust and ice particles.
The United Nations proclaimed June 30 as International Asteroid Day in 2016.

disputed: Whether Lake Cheko is an impact crater formed by a surviving fragment of the asteroid; scripts should attribute this claim to proposing Italian researchers rather than stating it as a settled fact.

Whether the incoming body was definitively a comet or a stony/iron asteroid; scripts should note that modern consensus leans toward an asteroid air burst, while acknowledging historical comet theories.
